newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares open lower as market jitters return.
newsitem.headline: German shares open lower as market jitters return.

text.p: The Frankfurt bourse opened lower on Wednesday with worries creeping back into the market of a fresh fall on Wall Street.
Dealers said the fact that S&P futures, which give an indication of how Wall Street would open, were down was worrying the market, along with losses on Asian markets overnight.
"The S&P contract has been doing funny things overnight and that has spooked some people," said one trader.
The DAX index of 30 top German shares, was down 44.86 points, or 1.55 percent, at 2,846.14 points by 0954 GMT.
The DAX had closed on Tuesday at 2,891 points, almost recouping all the losses posted on Friday following a bout of global market jitters.
Dealers said the fall on Friday, promted by comments by Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan about "irrational exuberance" in global asset markets, was still causing nerves.
"Greenspan is still making people edgy. We are extra-sensitive to any move down," said one trader.
The losses were spread across the board, with export-oriented chemicals and auto stocks especially hard hit as the dollar slipped below 1.55 marks.

Shares in drugs company Schering AG lost the most ground amongst the DAX stocks, slipping over three percent, or 4.50 marks to 126 marks, while car maker BMW AG was down 2.5 percent, or 27 marks to 1,050 marks.

Shares in chemicals and drugs company Hoechst AG were down 80 pfennigs at 71.70 marks, slightly less than the market trend and less than other chemical stocks after the firm made a buy out bid for French pharmaceuticals group Roussel Uclaf.
The stock had risen to a record high on Tuesday after the firm said it had merged its speciality chemicals division with the Swiss group Clariant AG.
Dealers said the market focus would turn to key inflation data due out of the U.S. later in the day, particularly in the light of worries following Greenspan's comments.
The market is particularly eager to see the U.S. November producer prices, forecast to show a 0.3 percent rise after climbing 0.4 percent in October.
